name: Online Freelancing and Remote Work from Africa
objectives: Using a list of your own skills, choose one service you can sell online and write it as a one-line offer, saying what you do, for whom and what the client gets

chapters.name: Chapter 1: Getting ready to work online

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Choosing a service you can sell
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose one service and write it as a one-line offer.
This lesson builds toward: Using a list of your own skills, you will choose one service you can sell online and write it as a one-line offer, saying what you do, for whom and what the client gets.
Freelancing means doing paid work for clients, one job at a time, instead of working for one employer. Remote work means a job, full-time or part-time, done from home or anywhere online. Both start with a skill clients need.
List what you can already do: writing, translating between English, French, Arabic or a local language, typing and data entry, using Excel or Google Sheets, graphic design on Canva, social media, customer support, bookkeeping, transcription, tutoring. Choose ONE to start; clients hire specialists.
Write a one-line offer: what you do, for whom, and what they get. Example: "I translate business documents from English to French for small companies, accurately and within 48 hours." Example: Kofi in Accra: "I design simple Canva flyers and social media posts for shops and churches."
If you need more skills, use free training. Kenya's government runs Ajira Digital for online work, and Nigeria's 3MTT programme trains young people in skills such as data, design and software.
Step by step:
- List five things you can do for others.
- Circle the one you do best and enjoy.
- Ask: who pays for this?
- Write: I do [what] for [whom] so they get [result].
- If you need more skill, look for free training.
Words to know:
- Freelancer: a person who does paid work for clients one job at a time.
- Remote work: a job done online from home or anywhere.
- Service offer: one sentence saying what you do, for whom and what they get.
Official sources:
- Kenya News Agency: youth urged to embrace the Ajira Digital Program (government programme for online work)
- 3MTT (3 Million Technical Talent), Nigeria: Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy with NITDA
Try it now: List five things you can do for others. Choose one and write your one-line offer: I do [what] for [whom] so they get [result].
You can now choose one service and describe it in a clear one-line offer.

check.q: Which is the clearest one-line offer?
options: "I type handwritten forms into Excel for clinics, accurately and fast"
check.why: It says what, for whom and what the client gets.

check.q: Why choose ONE service to start?
check.why: A clear specialty is easier for clients to trust and hire.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Your profile and a small portfolio
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a profile headline and overview and add two or three work samples.
This lesson builds toward: On a platform or a simple online page, you will write a profile headline and overview and add two or three small work samples, with no private details and samples you made yourself.
Your profile is your shop window. A headline says your service in a few words: "English-French Translator for Business Documents". The overview, a few short paragraphs, says who you help, what you do, how you work and one proof such as a past job or training.
Clients want proof. A portfolio is a few samples of your work. If you have no clients yet, make samples yourself: translate a short public notice, design a flyer for an imaginary shop, clean a small example spreadsheet. Never use another person's work, and never share real client information without permission.
Keep private details off your profile: no home address, ID number or bank details. Use a clear, friendly photo if the platform asks for one.
Save data: write your profile in a notes app first, then paste it in once. Compress images before uploading. Example: Mariam in Casablanca writes her Arabic-French profile offline, then uploads it at a cyber café in ten minutes.
Step by step:
- Write a headline: your service in a few words.
- Write the overview: who you help, what you do, how you work, one proof.
- Make two or three small samples yourself.
- Check: no private details, no one else's work.
- Write it offline first, then paste it in.
Words to know:
- Profile: your page on a platform that tells clients who you are and what you do.
- Portfolio: a few samples of your work that prove your skill.
- Headline: a short line under your name that says your service.
Try it now: Write your headline and a short overview in a notes app. Then make one small work sample for your service, for example a translated paragraph, a flyer or a cleaned spreadsheet.
You can now write a clear profile and show your skill with small work samples.

check.q: You have no clients yet. How can you build a portfolio?
options: Use a friend's work with your name
Wait until a client hires you
check.why: Samples you make yourself are honest proof of your skill.

check.q: What should NOT go on your profile?
options: Your home address and ID number
check.why: Private details can be misused; your profile needs only your skills and proof.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Finding jobs and writing a proposal
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a short proposal that answers a client's need.
This lesson builds toward: Given a job post, you will write a short proposal that answers the client's need, shows a related sample and asks one question, in under 150 words, written for that post, not copied.
Places to find work: freelance platforms (such as Upwork and Fiverr), LinkedIn, job boards, and people you know, such as local businesses, churches, NGOs and schools that need help online. Your first clients are often near you.
Read the job post twice. Find the client's need, the deadline and any question they ask. Skip posts that are vague, pay nothing or ask you to pay.
A proposal is your short reply. Keep it under 150 words: 1. Show you understood the need in one sentence. 2. Say how you will do it. 3. Point to one related sample. 4. Ask one useful question. Write it for that post; clients can spot a copied message.
Example: a client needs 200 product names typed into a spreadsheet. Ngozi in Lagos writes: "You need 200 product names and prices typed into a spreadsheet by Friday. I will type and double-check each row. Here is a sample sheet I made. Should prices be in naira or dollars?"
Step by step:
- Read the post twice; note the need, deadline and any question.
- Skip vague posts or any that ask you to pay.
- Sentence 1: the client's need in your words.
- Sentence 2: how you will do it.
- Add one related sample.
- Ask one useful question.
- Keep it under 150 words.
Words to know:
- Job post: a client's description of the work they need.
- Proposal: your short reply to a job post, saying how you will do the work.
Try it now: Find one real job post for your service (or use the spreadsheet example). Write a proposal of under 150 words with the four parts.
You can now write a short proposal that shows a client you understood their need.

check.q: What should the first sentence of a proposal do?
options: Show you understood the client's need
check.why: Showing you understood the need gets the client's attention.

check.q: Why write each proposal for that job post?
options: Clients can spot a copied message and skip it
check.why: A proposal written for the post shows care and understanding.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Doing the work and getting paid

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Agreeing the work and delivering on time
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Agree the scope, price, deadline and changes in writing before you start.
This lesson builds toward: Before you start a job, you will agree the scope, price, deadline and number of changes in writing and deliver on time, with a backup plan for power or data cuts.
Before you start, agree in writing (in the platform's messages or a short email) four things: the scope (exactly what you will deliver), the price, the deadline (with the time zone), and how many rounds of changes are included.
Example: "Scope: design 3 social media posts for your bakery. Price: as agreed in the contract. Deadline: Thursday 5 pm your time (London). Changes: up to 2 rounds." If the client later asks for more, politely offer a new price for the extra work.
Plan for power and data cuts. Charge your phone and a power bank, save work often to cloud storage, know a backup place to work (cyber café, hub, library), and do not leave work to the last day. If something goes wrong, tell the client early and honestly; most clients accept a short delay they hear about in advance.
Example: Ibrahima in Thiès works from 6 am, before the power cuts usually start, and keeps a copy of every file in Google Drive.
Step by step:
- Write the scope: exactly what you will deliver.
- Write the price and deadline, with the time zone.
- Write how many rounds of changes are included.
- Get the client's yes in writing.
- Save work often; keep a power and data backup.
- If you will be late, tell the client early.
Words to know:
- Scope: exactly what work you will deliver.
- Time zone: the local time in a place; London, Lagos and Nairobi can differ by hours.
- Revision: a change the client asks for after seeing your work.
Try it now: Write a short scope message for a job in your service: scope, price (as an example), deadline with time zone, and rounds of changes. Then write your backup plan for a power or data cut.
You can now agree a job's scope, price, deadline and changes in writing, and deliver on time with a backup plan.

check.q: Which is NOT one of the four things to agree before starting?
check.why: Scope, price, deadline and changes are the four.

check.q: The power is out and you may miss tomorrow's deadline. What do you do?
options: Tell the client early and give a new time
Ask the client for more money
check.why: Early, honest news keeps the client's trust.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Getting paid and keeping records
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose a safe way to be paid and record every payment.
This lesson builds toward: After you agree a job, you will choose a safe way to be paid and keep a record of every payment, keeping work and payment inside the platform when you use one, and recording each payment within a week.
On a platform, keep the work, the messages and the payment inside the platform. Its payment protection only works there. Clients who ask you to move off the platform to pay you "directly" are often scammers, and it can break the platform's rules.
Platforms pay out in different ways: to a bank account, to services such as Payoneer, or by other methods. What works depends on the platform and your country, and fees change. Read the payment and fees pages in the platform's own help centre before you take your first job.
With direct clients you know, agree how they pay before you start: bank transfer or mobile money, and when (for example half before and half on delivery). Deliver a sample or preview first if you are unsure.
Record every payment: date, client, job, amount and currency (USD, EUR, KES, NGN, GHS, XOF, MAD), fees and the amount you received. Online income can be taxed. Ask your national tax authority, for example the Kenya Revenue Authority or the Ghana Revenue Authority, or a tax adviser, what you must register and pay.
Step by step:
- On a platform, keep work and payment inside it.
- Read the platform's own payment and fees pages.
- With direct clients, agree how and when they pay before you start.
- Record each payment within a week: date, client, job, amount, currency, fees, received.
- Ask the national tax authority what applies to you.
Words to know:
- Payment protection: a platform's system that holds or guarantees payment for work done inside it.
- Currency: the type of money: US dollars, euros, naira, cedis, shillings, CFA francs, dirhams.
- Tax authority: the government office that collects tax, such as KRA in Kenya or GRA in Ghana.
Official sources:
- Kenya Revenue Authority (income tax, including income earned online)
- Ghana Revenue Authority
Try it now: Make a payment record table with these columns: date, client, job, amount, currency, fees, amount received. Add one example row. Then find the payment help page of one platform you might use.
You can now choose a safe way to be paid, keep a record of every payment, and know where to ask about tax.

check.q: A new client on a platform asks you to move to WhatsApp and be paid "directly". What is the risk?
options: You lose the platform's payment protection, and it is often a scam
The platform will pay the fee
check.why: Payment protection only works inside the platform; off-platform requests are a common scam sign.

check.q: Who can tell you what tax you owe on online income?
options: Your national tax authority or a tax adviser
Nobody; online income is never taxed
check.why: Tax rules differ by country; the tax authority or an adviser can tell you.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Fake jobs and payment scams
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Identify fake job offers and name the warning sign in each.
This lesson builds toward: Given five job offers or messages, you will identify the fake ones and name the warning sign in each, getting at least 4 of 5 right, before you pay or share any details.
New freelancers are a big target. Warning signs: 1. They ask YOU to pay: for registration, training, a "starter kit" or software. 2. Pay that is too high for easy work, like "earn USD 500 a day liking videos". 3. They ask for your passwords, PIN, one-time codes or ID documents. 4. They want to move you off the platform at once. 5. They "overpay" by cheque or transfer and ask you to send the extra back. 6. "Task" or "investment" jobs where you deposit money to unlock tasks or earnings, often pushed on WhatsApp, Telegram and TikTok.
Nigeria's SEC has warned about schemes promoted on social media that promise high returns. Real clients pay you for work; they never ask you to pay to work.
Protect your accounts: a strong, different password for your email and each platform, two-step verification turned on, and never share codes. Do not let anyone "rent" or use your verified account; it can be used for fraud in your name.
Then put your starter pack together: your offer, profile, samples, one proposal, and your safety and payment checklist.
Step by step:
- Ask: do they want me to pay?
- Ask: is the pay too good for the work?
- Ask: do they want passwords, codes or ID?
- Ask: are they rushing me off the platform?
- Any yes: stop, do not pay, report it to the platform.
- Turn on two-step verification and never share codes.
Words to know:
- Overpayment scam: a fake payment of too much money, then a request to send the extra back before the fake payment bounces.
- Two-step verification: a second check, such as a code to your phone, when you log in.
- Task scam: a fake job where you must deposit money to unlock tasks or earnings.
Official sources:
- Nairametrics (14 May 2026): SEC Nigeria warns against schemes promoted on WhatsApp, TikTok and Instagram
Try it now: Final task: put together your freelance starter pack: one-line offer, profile headline and overview, two or three samples, one proposal to a real or sample job post, and a checklist with your payment method, your record table, where you will ask about tax and the six fake-job warning signs.
You can now spot fake jobs and payment scams and present yourself as a ready-to-hire freelancer.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Clear offer The offer is vague ("I do everything online"). One service, saying what you do, for whom and what the client gets. The offer names a specific type of client and a clear result or turnaround time. Profile and samples No headline or overview, no samples, or private details shown. Headline, short overview and two or three samples the learner made, with no private details. Samples match the offer closely and the overview includes one proof (training or a past job). Proposal Long, copied or does not mention the client's need. Under 150 words, written for the post: the need, how, one sample, one question. The question shows real thought about the job, and the proposal fits the client's tone. Agreeing the work No written scope or deadline. A scope message with scope, price, deadline with time zone and changes, plus a power or data backup plan. Also includes how extra work will be priced. Payment and records No payment method or record table. A safe payment method (inside the platform, or agreed in advance with a known client), a record table, and where to ask about tax. The payment method was checked on the platform's own help page. Scam awareness Fewer than four warning signs, or plans to pay a fee to get work. Lists the six fake-job warning signs and says two-step verification is on. Adds a real fake offer the learner saw and how they spotted it. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: A "recruiter" offers a data entry job but asks for USD 20 for a starter kit. What is the warning sign?
options: They ask you to pay to work
check.why: Real clients pay you; asking you to pay is the classic fake-job sign.

check.q: A client sends more than the agreed amount and asks you to send the extra back quickly. What is this?
check.why: The first payment is often fake and bounces after you send your own money back.
